newsitem.title: USA: Mergers create new jitters in the marketing department.
newsitem.headline: Mergers create new jitters in the marketing department.

text.p: Marketing has been singled out for the surgeon's scalpel in a number of recent corporate mergers, causing job losses for many staff people and uncertainty in the ad industry.
The marketing cutbacks are dramatic in two announced business consolidations.

In a contemplated merger of refining and marketing operations of three giant refiners, Texaco Inc., Shell Oil Company and Star Enterprise, which would include 22,000 gasoline stations, much of the expected $800 million savings would come in reduced and refocused marketing.

In another recent merger, between Staples Inc., and Office Depot Inc., which would create by far the biggest office-products company, cost reductions in advertising and marketing will approximate $205 million in the next three years, much higher than in any other phase of the combined corporations.

In some cases, the advertising reductions have been so drastic that they have affected the revenues and profits of such major media as The New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, the Boston Globe, CBS Broadcasting, other television networks, more than a few radio stations and many smaller players in the print and airborne media.
Because of duplication of marketing, advertising and public relations departments, lots of practitioners in those fields have suddenly found themselves out on the street after many years of service.

"I've never seen any corporate activity that CEO's didn't think they knew as well as marketing, which makes it such an easy target," said Robert Nesbit, senior partner, Korn/Ferry International, New York, the nation's leading executive recruiter.

"If you are advertising two separate product groups, say, to the extent of $100 million each, it makes sense to consolidate it all to gain economy-of-scale benefits," said Alfred Schreiber, senior partner, Bozell Worldwide, the New York-based advertising agency.

"That is, when there's no longer a need for a separate identification for each. But when two brands come under one umbrella and are still viable, I certainly wouldn't recommend cutting their advertising," Schreiber said.

Often, however, when it comes to retaining people, it becomes a game of "the conqueror and the conquered. The acquirer tends to favour those he brings with him when it should really be a matter of operating on a merit basis instead of rewarding those people lucky enough to be on the winning side," he added.

A new trend also developing in mergers among companies with well-known brands is that the corporation that survives is now taking pains to market its own name as well as the brands of products and services it sells, the Bozell executive noted.

"Companies like Sony or American Express not only are spending on their product/service brands but also on their corporate names because they know it has value and brand equity of its own," Schreiber said.

An experienced executive recruiter, Hal Rider of Herb Mines & Associates, New York, said head counts represent a significant amount of costs in both administration and marketing and therefore become heavily impacted in mergers.
"I think it's fair to say that more merchandising and marketing people are being dislocated in mergers than any other type of employee," he said.

Euphemistically, perhaps, some companies involved in mergers prefer to term cost-cutting as "synergies." This is the case with the ongoing Staples-Office Depot deal, in which both managements spelled out the details of the merger early in September. Among the "synergies" they cited will be savings in advertising and marketing of $31 million the first year, $41 million the second and $76 million in the third year. No further details on these cuts were given.

All those interviewed were certain that the trend of chopping off big chunks of the marketing function and the heads of those who work in it will continue as long as the merger trend is sustained. With that trend apparently at one of its highs, their recommendation is simply to work for a winner.
